catalog_quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature of the YMA lexical phonology: no pair of words contrasts only by the syllable on which stress falls. We will see below that stress does play a role at the prosodic level, though, helping to distinguish between declarative and question clauses. Except for a few noteworthy exceptions discussed later, the stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable at the lexical level. This tendency applies both to morphologically simple items, such as roots, and to more complex ones, such as derived or inflected stems. ... The nouns with classifiers (free word plus classifier) constitute phonological units in the language. Following the tendency of the language, the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable. ... In all these complex nominal phrases, the stress still falls on the penultimate syllable. ... In polysyllabic roots, the stress occurs on the penult…

(2) Deciding source is the 2017 LOT/Radboud dissertation grammar (779 pp over 2 vols), Glottolog's only 'grammar' for the language and the most recent and detailed description; its stress section is impressionistic but explicit, with nominal clitic strings, verbs and listed exceptions. Two independent held sources agree: Migliazza 1972 p. 190 (Yanomam = Language B: primary stress on the penultimate vowel of the word, emphatic shift to final in verbs, secondary stress two syllables before) and Dixon & Aikhenvald 1999 ch. 13 (penult primary, alternating secondary). Nothing seen contradicts the penult coding; Migliazza adds a secondary

sources.quote: Ja vimos que o padrao silabico dos dialetos estudados e de tipo (C) V e, portanto,nao existem silabas fechadas. No entanto,as vogais atonas (finais ou nao finais) tornam-se muitas vezes surdas e quase inaudiveis. Em discurso rapido, estas vogais podem cair: ke-rayo-ma "caiu" [kera'yomA]~[ke'rayOma]~[kera'yom]~[ke'rayma]; ma+ u pe "agua" [ma+'upE]~[ma+'up]~[ma+'uP]; ware k+k+ "queixadas" [ware'k+k+]~[ware k+k]; koraha si "bananeira" [kora'hasI]~[kora'has] ... koraha si pe "bananeiras" [koraha'sip] [estilo rapido]

sources.quote: 'Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of underlying forms of words. B.P.1 Same as A.P.1. However, when focusing or in emphatic speech especially in verbs (adjectivals and adverbials, etc.) stress is shifted to the last vowel. ... Secondary stress is placed on the second syllable preceding the stressed one.'

tone.quote: 2. There are four intonation contours: rising, falling-rising, mid-rising and incomplete, each occurring over one or more feet. The rising contour occurs over one, two or three feet. It begins on a low pitch, rises to high on the penultimate or final syllable of the last foot and falls off rapidly to a mid pitch. [...] The loudest point of the crescendo coincides with the highest point of the intonation contour, and with the stress of the final foot in the contour. [...] 3.0. Morphophonemically, foot stress is part of the representation of certain morphemes, and the distribution of variants of intonation contours is predictable in terms of the grammatical sequences they occur with.
